title: Part 1, Chapter 24
paragraphs: In which the adventure of the Sierra Morena continues
The history tells us that Don Quixote listened with the closest attention to the ragged knight of the Sierra, who began by saying:

“Whoever you are, señor — for I don’t know you — I sincerely thank you for the kindness and courtesy you have shown me, and I wish I were in a position to repay you with something more than goodwill for the warm welcome you have given me; but my fate leaves me no other way of returning the favors done to me except a heartfelt desire to repay them.”

“Mine,” Don Quixote replied, “is to be of service to you — so much so that I had made up my mind not to leave these mountains until I had found you and learned from you whether any kind of relief exists for the sorrow that, judging by the strangeness of your life, you seem to suffer from; and I meant to search for you with all possible diligence, if searching had been necessary. And if your misfortune turned out to be the kind that refuses any sort of consolation, I intended to join you in grieving and mourning over it as far as I could, for it is still some comfort in misfortune to find someone who can feel it with you. And if my good intentions deserve to be acknowledged with any kind of courtesy, I beg you, señor, by the courtesy I can see you possess in such abundance — and I likewise implore you by whatever you love or have loved most in this life — to tell me who you are, and what cause has brought you to live or die in these wild solitudes like a brute animal, dwelling among them in a way so foreign to your station, as your clothing and appearance make plain. And I swear,” Don Quixote added, “by the order of knighthood I have received and by my vocation as a knight-errant, that if you grant me this, I will serve you with all the dedication my calling demands of me — either by relieving your misfortune, if it admits of relief, or by joining you in lamenting it, as I promised to do.”

When the Knight of the Thicket heard the Knight of the Rueful Countenance talk in this way, he did nothing but stare at him, then stare at him again, and look him over from head to foot; and when he had examined him thoroughly, he said to him:
“If you have anything to give me to eat, then for God’s sake give it to me. Once I have eaten, I will do everything you ask, in gratitude for the goodwill you have shown me.”

Sancho dug into his sack and the goatherd into his pouch, and between them they gave the Ragged One the means of satisfying his hunger. He ate what they offered like a man out of his mind, so fast that he left no pause between mouthfuls — gulping his food down rather than swallowing it — and while he ate, neither he nor those watching him said a word. As soon as he finished, he signaled for them to follow him, which they did, and he led them to a patch of green grass a little farther on, around the corner of a rock. When they reached it, he stretched out on the grass, and the others did the same, all in silence, until the Ragged One, settling himself in his place, said:

“If you want me, gentlemen, to describe in a few words the enormous scope of my misfortunes, you must promise not to break the thread of my sad story with any question or other interruption, because the moment you do, the tale I am telling will come to an end.”

These words from the Ragged One reminded Don Quixote of the story his squire had told him, when he failed to keep count of the goats that had crossed the river and the tale was left unfinished. But to return to the Ragged One — he went on to say:

“I give you this warning because I want to pass quickly over the story of my misfortunes; calling them back to memory only adds new ones, and the less you question me, the sooner I will finish the account — though I won’t leave out anything important, so as to satisfy your curiosity in full.”
Don Quixote gave the promise on behalf of himself and the others, and with that assurance the man began as follows:

“My name is Cardenio; my birthplace is one of the finest cities of this Andalusia; my family is noble; my parents are rich; and my misfortune is so great that my parents must have wept over it and my family grieved, without all their wealth being able to lighten it — because the gifts of fortune can do little against the reverses Heaven sends. In that same region there was a heaven in which love had placed all the glory I could wish for: such was the beauty of Luscinda, a young woman as noble and as rich as I am, but luckier in her fortunes, and less constant than a love as worthy as mine deserved. I loved this Luscinda, worshipped her, adored her, from my earliest and tenderest years, and she loved me with all the innocence and sincerity of childhood. Our parents knew how we felt and were not sorry to see it, for they could tell plainly that as our feelings matured they would have to end in marriage between us — something that seemed almost arranged in advance by the equal standing of our families and our wealth. We grew up, and our love grew with us, so much so that Luscinda’s father felt obliged, for propriety’s sake, to bar me from his house — in this perhaps imitating the parents of that Thisbe the poets have made so famous. The ban only added love to love and flame to flame, because though they could force silence on our tongues, they could not impose it on our pens, which reveal the heart’s secrets to the one you love more freely than tongues can; for the presence of the person you love often shakes the firmest resolve and strikes the boldest tongue dumb. Heavens, how many letters I wrote her, and how many delicate, modest replies I received! How many songs and love poems I composed, in which my heart declared and laid bare its feelings, described its burning longings, lingered over its memories, and toyed with its desires! At last, growing impatient and feeling my heart wasting away with the longing to see her, I decided to act on what seemed to me the best way of winning the reward I desired and deserved: to ask her father for her hand as my lawful wife. And I did. His answer was that he thanked me for the honor I showed in wanting to ally myself with him and to consider myself honored by the gift of his treasure; but since my father was alive, the request was rightfully his to make — because if the match were not entirely according to his will and pleasure, Luscinda was not a woman to be taken or given in secret. I thanked him for his kindness, thinking there was sense in what he said and that my father would agree to it the moment I told him; and with that in mind, I went that very instant to let my father know what I wanted. When I entered the room where he was, I found him with an open letter in his hand, and before I could say a word he handed it to me, saying, ‘This letter will show you, Cardenio, how ready Duke Ricardo is to do you a service.’ This Duke Ricardo, as you gentlemen probably know already, is a grandee of Spain whose seat lies in the best part of this Andalusia. I took the letter and read it, and it was worded so flatteringly that even I felt it would be wrong of my father not to grant what the duke asked in it — which was that my father send me to him immediately, because he wanted me to be the companion, not the servant, of his eldest son, and would take it upon himself to place me in a position matching the esteem in which he held me. Reading the letter left me speechless, and I was struck dumber still when I heard my father say, ‘Two days from now you will set out, Cardenio, as the duke wishes; and give thanks to God, who is opening a road for you toward what I know you deserve’ — and to these words he added others of fatherly advice. The day of my departure came. I spoke to Luscinda one night and told her everything that had happened, and I told her father too, begging him to allow some delay and to put off deciding her hand until I saw what Duke Ricardo wanted of me. He gave me his promise, and she confirmed it with countless vows and fainting fits. Finally, I presented myself to the duke, who received and treated me so kindly that envy very soon got to work: the old servants grew jealous of me and took the duke’s inclination to favor me as an injury to themselves. But the person my arrival pleased most was the duke’s second son, Fernando by name — a dashing young man, noble, generous, and amorous by temperament — who very quickly made me such a close friend that everyone remarked on it. Though the elder son liked me and treated me kindly, he never carried his affection to the lengths Don Fernando did. Now, since no secret stays unshared between friends, and since the favor I enjoyed with Don Fernando had grown into real friendship, he told me all his thoughts, and in particular a love affair that was troubling him somewhat. He was deeply in love with a peasant girl, one of his father’s vassals, the daughter of wealthy parents — and herself so beautiful, modest, sensible, and virtuous that no one who knew her could decide in which of these qualities she was most gifted or most excelled. The fair peasant girl’s attractions drove Don Fernando’s passion to such a pitch that, in order to get what he wanted and overcome her virtuous resistance, he decided to pledge his word to her that he would become her husband — since trying it any other way was attempting the impossible. Bound to him as I was by friendship, I did my best, with the strongest arguments and the most forceful examples I could think of, to hold him back and talk him out of such a course; but seeing I was getting nowhere, I resolved to inform his father, Duke Ricardo, of the matter. Don Fernando, however, being sharp and shrewd, foresaw and feared exactly this, realizing that as a loyal servant I was duty-bound not to keep hidden something so damaging to the honor of my lord the duke. And so, to mislead and deceive me, he told me he could find no better way of driving from his mind the beauty that so enslaved him than to go away for a few months — and that he wanted the absence to take the form of the two of us going together to my father’s house, under the pretext, which he would give the duke, of going to see and buy some fine horses in my city, which produces the best in the world. The moment I heard him say it — even if his plan had been less sound — my own feelings would have made me hail it as one of the happiest ideas imaginable, seeing what a perfect chance and opportunity it offered me to go back and see my Luscinda. With that thought and that wish, I applauded his idea and encouraged his plan, urging him to carry it out as quickly as possible, since absence does its work, in truth, against even the most deeply rooted feelings. But, as it later turned out, when he said all this to me he had already enjoyed the peasant girl under the title of husband, and was only waiting for a chance to reveal it safely, afraid of what his father the duke would do when he learned of his folly. Now, with young men, love is for the most part nothing more than appetite, and since appetite’s final goal is pleasure, it ends the moment it obtains it, and what seemed to be love takes flight — because it cannot pass the limit nature sets, a limit nature sets nowhere for true love. What I mean is that once Don Fernando had enjoyed the peasant girl, his passion subsided and his eagerness cooled; and if at first he pretended to want to go away in order to cure his love, he was now genuinely eager to leave in order to avoid keeping his promise.

“The duke gave him permission and ordered me to go with him. We arrived at my city, and my father gave him the reception his rank deserved. I saw Luscinda without delay, and my love — though it had never been dead or even dulled — gained fresh life. To my sorrow, I told the whole story of it to Don Fernando, because it seemed to me that under the law of the great friendship he showed me, I was bound to hide nothing from him. I praised her beauty, her liveliness, her wit, so warmly that my praises stirred in him a desire to see a young woman graced with such attractions. To my misfortune, I gave in to it, and showed her to him one night by the light of a candle, at a window where she and I used to talk. He saw her in her dressing gown, and she drove every beauty he had seen until then out of his memory. He was struck speechless; his head spun; he was spellbound; and in the end he was lovesick, as you will see as the story of my misfortune unfolds. And to inflame his passion further — a passion he hid from me and confessed only to Heaven — it happened that one day he found a note of hers begging me to ask her father for her hand in marriage, a note so delicate, so modest, and so tender that on reading it he told me that in Luscinda alone were gathered all the charms of beauty and intelligence that were scattered among all the other women in the world. It is true — and I admit it now — that although I knew how much reason Don Fernando had to praise Luscinda, it unsettled me to hear those praises from his mouth, and I began to fear him, and with good reason to distrust him, because there was no moment when he wasn’t ready to talk about Luscinda; he would bring up the subject himself, even dragging it in where it didn’t belong — which woke a certain jealousy in me. Not that I feared any change in Luscinda’s constancy or faithfulness; but even so, my fate made me dread the very thing she kept assuring me against. Don Fernando always contrived to read the letters I sent Luscinda and her replies to me, on the pretext that he enjoyed the wit and intelligence of us both. So it happened that Luscinda, having asked me for a book of chivalry to read — one she was very fond of, Amadis of Gaul—”
The moment Don Quixote heard a book of chivalry mentioned, he said:

“If your worship had told me at the start of your story that the Lady Luscinda was fond of books of chivalry, no other praise would have been needed to convince me of the superiority of her mind — for it could not have been as excellent as you describe if she had lacked a taste for such delightful reading. So as far as I am concerned, you need not waste another word describing her beauty, worth, and intelligence: just from hearing what her taste is, I declare her the most beautiful and the most intelligent woman in the world. And I wish your worship had sent her, along with Amadis of Gaul, the worthy Don Rugel of Greece, because I know the Lady Luscinda would thoroughly enjoy Daraida and Garaya, and the shrewd sayings of the shepherd Darinel, and the wonderful verses of his pastoral songs, which he sang and delivered with such liveliness, wit, and ease. But a time may come when that omission can be put right, and to fix it nothing more is needed than for your worship to be kind enough to come with me to my village, where I can give you more than three hundred books that are the delight of my soul and the entertainment of my life — though now that I think of it, I do not have a single one of them left, thanks to the spite of wicked and envious enchanters. But forgive me for breaking the promise we made not to interrupt your account; when I hear chivalry or knights-errant mentioned, I can no more help talking about them than the sun’s rays can help giving heat, or the moon’s giving moisture. So forgive me, and go on — that is what matters most now.”

While Don Quixote was saying this, Cardenio let his head drop onto his chest and seemed sunk in deep thought; and though Don Quixote twice urged him to go on with his story, he neither looked up nor answered a word. But after a while he raised his head and said, “I cannot get the idea out of my head — and no one in the world will remove it or make me think otherwise, and anyone who holds or believes anything else is a blockhead — that that utter scoundrel Master Elisabad was carrying on with Queen Madasima.”

“That is not true, by all that’s good,” said Don Quixote in a fury, rounding on him angrily, as his way was. “It is an outrageous slander — or rather, a villainy. Queen Madasima was a most illustrious lady, and it is unthinkable that so exalted a princess would have carried on with a quack; and whoever claims the contrary lies like a complete scoundrel, and I will make him know it, on foot or on horseback, armed or unarmed, by night or by day, or however he likes best.”

Cardenio was staring at him fixedly. His mad fit had now come over him, and he had no inclination to go on with his story — nor would Don Quixote have listened to it, so thoroughly had what he heard about Madasima disgusted him. Strangely enough, he defended her as if she were truly and literally his own born lady; that is the state his unholy books had brought him to. Cardenio, then, being mad as I said, heard himself called a liar and a scoundrel and other insulting names, and did not take the joke well: he snatched up a stone he found near him and struck Don Quixote such a blow on the chest with it that he knocked him flat on his back. Sancho Panza, seeing his master treated this way, went at the madman with his fists clenched; but the Ragged One met him with a punch that stretched him out at his feet, and then climbed on top of him and crushed his ribs to his own satisfaction. The goatherd, who came to the rescue, got the same treatment; and once he had beaten and pounded them all, he left them and calmly withdrew to his hiding place in the mountains. Sancho got up, and in his rage at being thrashed so badly without deserving it, ran to take his revenge on the goatherd, accusing him of failing to warn them that this man was sometimes seized by fits of madness — because if they had known, they would have been on their guard to protect themselves. The goatherd replied that he had said so, and that if Sancho had not heard him, that was no fault of his. Sancho shot back, the goatherd answered him, and the argument ended with the two of them grabbing each other by the beard and trading such punches that if Don Quixote had not made peace between them, they would have beaten each other to pieces.

“Leave me alone, Sir Knight of the Rueful Countenance,” said Sancho, grappling with the goatherd. “This fellow is a commoner like me, not a dubbed knight, so I can safely take satisfaction for the insult he has done me, fighting him hand to hand like an honest man.”
“True enough,” said Don Quixote, “but I know that he is not to blame for what has happened here.”

With that he calmed them down, and again asked the goatherd whether it would be possible to find Cardenio, because he felt the keenest anxiety to learn how his story ended. The goatherd told him, as he had told him before, that there was no knowing for certain where his lair was; but that if he roamed around that neighborhood long enough, he could not fail to come across him, in or out of his senses.
